summary:
Mission Trainer is a free, browser-based turn-based strategy game for young learners that teaches how a crew survives on the Moon. The player manages a lunar base for 30 sols. Each turn they balance power, oxygen, water, food and crew tasks, and they must prepare the base to survive the long, cold lunar night, when solar power is unavailable.
The game answers the “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” challenge by turning real mission constraints into simple decisions. Players learn why energy storage, life support and careful planning matter, and they see the consequences of poor choices in a safe environment. No installation or account is required: it runs in any modern browser on a computer or phone.
It matters because it makes space exploration engaging and understandable for students, and it builds systems thinking and resource-management skills that are useful far beyond the game.
details:
Mission Trainer is a free, browser-based, turn-based strategy game that teaches young learners how a crew survives on the Moon. The player runs a lunar base for 30 days. Every turn they allocate resources and crew time across power, life support and base maintenance. The central challenge is the lunar night: the base must store enough energy before sunlight disappears, or the crew will not make it through.

How it works: the game state is updated turn by turn from the player’s decisions, and the outcomes (shortages, failures, survival) are shown immediately so players learn cause and effect.

Benefits and intended impact: the game turns real mission constraints into simple, memorable decisions. It builds systems thinking and planning skills, and it makes space exploration approachable for students and teachers. It needs no installation or account and runs on a computer or phone.

Creativity: instead of a quiz, learning happens through play. Failure is safe, and every run teaches why energy storage and preparation matter for long-term lunar presence.

Tools: TypeScript, Vite, HTML/CSS, automated tests (npm test), GitHub for the repository and GitHub Pages for hosting.

Factors we considered: simple rules for junior players, short sessions, accessibility on any device, and scientific plausibility over entertainment value alone.
